strengths: The paper presents a clean, well-motivated unified architecture (native joint self-attention) that avoids costly cross-modal fusion modules, and the ablation in Table 5 convincingly demonstrates its superiority over sequential and parallel cross-attention variants under matched capacity/data.

The channel-wise conditioning strategy for visual references is a sensible engineering solution to avoid token-length explosion, and it elegantly unifies image-to-video generation and video editing without architectural changes.

The mouth-area loss is simple yet effective, with a thorough ablation (Table 4) showing a dramatic LSE-C improvement (1.39 to 6.70) and, notably, an appendix validation (zero-masking in latent space) that convincingly verifies the mouth region is correctly localized in latent space.

The paper contributes a large, well-documented ~3M-sample training corpus with clear data construction pipelines (Fig. 3) for both generation and editing, plus two new benchmarks (JoVABench-Gen/Edit) with explicit train/test overlap filtering.

Extensive experiments span three benchmarks (JoVABench-Gen, JoVABench-Edit, Verse-Bench) plus VBench for pure video quality and a human subjective study (MOS), covering many quality dimensions (lip-sync, audio quality, video fidelity, instruction-following) with consistent state-of-the-art or highly competitive results and supporting qualitative examples.
Reasonable, non-inflated limitations discussion (finger artifacts, text preservation in edits, lack of general-scene editing data) that appropriately scopes claims rather than overselling.
weaknesses: No comparison exists against a true end-to-end joint video-audio editing baseline; the editing evaluation is against cascaded pipelines (video editor + lip-sync model fed ground-truth audio), which is an easier task, making the head-to-head claims less rigorous than the generation comparisons.

Because JoVA is built on top of a pretrained 12B Waver backbone with additional proprietary data pipelines (GPT-4o, FLUX.1-Kontext, Wan2.2-Fun, Higgs-Audio, etc.), reproducibility is a real concern for the community absent public release of the model, training data, and benchmarks.

The training corpus construction relies heavily on synthetic/pseudo-labeled data (e.g., edited videos generated by FLUX.1-Kontext + Wan2.2-Fun-Control, synthetic speech via Higgs-Audio, lip-sync via an external module) which could introduce systematic biases or artifacts that propagate into the trained model and inflate self-benchmark scores (JoVABench-Edit is itself derived from a similar pipeline).

Some ablation studies (e.g., mouth-loss weight, fusion strategy) appear to be run only on JoVABench-Gen with a single set of hyperparameters/seeds; no variance/multiple-run statistics are reported, and the JoVABench-Edit categories (background/style/local) are not broken down quantitatively in the main comparison table.

The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior joint video-audio models (Ovi, UniAVGen, LTX-2): the core idea of replacing cross-attention with joint self-attention and reusing pretrained backbone parameters, while effective, is a natural extension rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and this should be more explicitly acknowledged.

Human evaluation involves a modest number of participants (21) and only 50 samples per task, which, combined with the paper's own benchmarks (rather than fully independent ones), limits the strength of the human-preference claims.
